title: The mountain of Moriah (Genesis 22:1–19)
hookLine: the hardest story: Abraham is tested, a ram is caught, and the place is named the Lord will provide

lines: NOT SOLVING IT, SITTING WITH IT.
cards: Some stories you can tell a child at bedtime. Some you can't. Genesis twenty-two is the second kind.
Jews call it the Akedah, the binding. Christians, Jews and Muslims each have their own tellings of a father asked to give up his son. Painters and philosophers keep coming back to it.
It is a hard text, and rereading doesn't make it softer. So today isn't about solving it; it's about reading it slowly and sitting with it.

teach.b: It opens, in the King James Bible: "God did tempt Abraham." Tempt here means test, and the reader is told that before Abraham knows anything. God calls, and Abraham answers, here am I.
Then the command, every phrase heavier than the last: "Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest." Go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there.
Early in the morning, Abraham saddles his donkey, and they walk for three days. Isaac carries the wood. Abraham carries the fire and the knife.
Isaac: "Behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Abraham: "My son, God will provide himself a lamb." And the two of them went together, the text says, twice.
At the top, Abraham builds the altar, binds his son, and lifts the knife, and the angel of the LORD calls his name twice: Abraham, Abraham. Lay not thine hand upon the lad.

teach.h: A RAM CAUGHT IN A THICKET.
teach.b: He looks up, and there is a ram caught in a thicket by its horns.
He names the place Jehovah-jireh, in the King James Bible: the LORD will see, the LORD will provide. In Hebrew it's the same verb as Hagar's El Roi, the God who sees. Readers answer it in many ways.
Jews read it at the new year and remember Abraham's faith and Isaac's binding.

teach.h: GOD WILL PROVIDE HIMSELF A LAMB.
teach.b: Christian tradition has heard Good Friday in it: a son carrying wood up a hill, and a lamb provided. And readers in each tradition have found it deeply troubling.
The text doesn't say what Abraham felt, how old Isaac was, or whether Sarah knew. That's the end of a week of promises: stars, a seeing God, strangers, a bargain, a laugh, a well, and this mountain.

how: Many churches read Genesis 22 during Lent or at the Easter Vigil, where it is heard alongside the story of Good Friday.

o: the LORD is my shepherd, from a psalm

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: caught in a thicket by its horns

s: the reader is told it's a test before Abraham knows anything
"God did tempt Abraham": in the King James English, tempt means test.
Genesis tells us Isaac's age and what Sarah knew
it tells us neither. it doesn't tell us what Abraham felt either.
Isaac carries the wood up the mountain
Isaac carries the wood; Abraham carries the fire and the knife.

games.q: you're Isaac, walking up the mountain carrying the wood. you see the fire and the knife, but no lamb. what do you do?
games.why: "behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Abraham answers: "my son, God will provide himself a lamb."

practice: You don't have to make sense of Moriah today; let it sit, unresolved, like a stone in your hand, beside anything in your own life you can't tie up.
Don't argue it closed or force a moral; keep breathing next to it, the way father and son walked together. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: Jehovah-jireh. The name Abraham gives the mountain: the Lord will see, the Lord will provide, after a ram is caught and Isaac is spared.

orig.note: Hebrew: will see, will provide, from the same verb as El Roi, the God who sees.

carryVoice: Your line: the lord will provide. A hard question can stay a question for now. That's the week.
